reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .416 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.69 xERA on the mound put the two-way argument beyond debate. The bat is built on genuine contact quality: 93.6 mph average exit velocity, a 17.1% barrel rate, and a 14.8% walk rate that lets him get to all of it, and his 22.9% strikeout rate means none of that leverage gets surrendered at the other end. On the mound, a 30.4% whiff rate and opponents averaging 87.4 mph exit velocity against him tells you the xERA isn't a lucky number waiting to correct. The projection, .285/.396/.555 with 39 home runs across 685 plate appearances, is what a healthy full season looks like, and the only real dependency is the body holding together for both halves of the job simultaneously, which is a risk nobody else in the sport even creates the conditions to take.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power case for James Wood lives entirely in the barrel numbers: a 22.7% barrel rate and 95.0 mph average exit velocity that both sit at the 100th percentile, and a .625 xSLG that says the power already translates at the highest level. The tension is the strikeout rate, 28.4% against a walk rate of 17.4%, which is an unusual pairing, elite plate discipline on one side and a 30.9% whiff rate on the other, and the profile hangs on whether he continues to sell out for contact enough that the walks keep outpacing the damage the swing-and-miss does to the average. If that holds, a projected .272/.395/.545 line with 42 home runs across 732 plate appearances is a true middle-of-the-order force. If the whiff rate climbs, what remains is still a high-OBP slugger worth building around.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The contact quality is loud enough that 46 projected home runs at age 22 isn't a stretch. At 93.2 mph average exit velocity with a 51.8% hard-hit rate, Caminero is hitting the ball with the kind of authority that earns a .372 xwOBA, and his 12.9% walk rate means pitchers don't get to pick their spots. The whole profile hinges on whether the strikeout rate stays where it is, because at 19.0% it's manageable, but if pitchers find a way to exploit him and that number climbs, the .908 OPS projection softens in a hurry. He's a corner bat with no defensive or speed safety net, which makes the bat carry everything, and right now, it can.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .311, 100th percentile, while the projection calls for a .288 average, meaning the bat-to-ball quality is actually running ahead of what he's projected to produce. Pair that with a 93.2 mph average exit velocity and 52.7% hard-hit rate, both in the 95th percentile, and you have a hitter whose contact profile is legitimately elite. The 33.2% chase rate is the one place the Statcast card whispers caution, sitting in the 28th percentile, and if pitchers keep expanding him successfully the projected .355 OBP is probably the ceiling rather than the floor. But 45 projected steals on a 99th-percentile 30.2 ft/s sprint speed means even a modest regression in plate discipline leaves a five-category monster on the field.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The gap between his .364 xwOBA and a 35.5% chase rate is the whole argument: elite contact quality sitting on top of a swing decision profile that costs him at-bats. His 48.6% hard-hit rate backs the expected slugging, and 11.2% walk rate shows genuine zone awareness when he doesn't expand, but chasing that often at 25.8% strikeout rate means he's leaving production on the table every week. Add 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and the projection's 38 steals with 32 home runs become credible, a 30-steal, 30-homer center fielder who hits .276 with a .361 OBP if the chase rate even nudges down — and something closer to a good-not-great corner-type offensive profile if it doesn't.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: A .474 xwOBA with a 100th-percentile ceiling on both expected average and expected slug tells you everything about where Alvarez sits relative to the rest of the sport. The contact quality is absurd: 94.7 mph average exit velocity, an 18.7% barrel rate, and more than half his balls in play qualify as hard-hit. What keeps this from being a walk-year outlier read is the discipline — a 15.0% walk rate and a 17.1% strikeout rate mean he's taking walks at an elite clip while making contact better than almost any hitter alive. The projection of .310/.419/.609 with 46 home runs in 680 plate appearances is just what the Statcast profile says he is, translated into a box score.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.71 and the strikeout rate at 29.5%, and together they say the same thing: Skenes is already pitching at ace level, not trending toward it. What's interesting is that the whiff rate, at 27.6%, is merely solid rather than historic, which means the strikeouts come from a combination of genuine swing-and-miss and a chase rate, 33.7%, that forces hitters into early counts they can't win. The projection fills in the rest cleanly, 183.5 innings with a 3.32 ERA, WHIP of 1.04, and 222 strikeouts, all of which track with a profile where contact, when it happens, tends to be weak. The whole thing hinges on innings health, because everything downstream depends on Skenes actually taking that workload at 23.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.40 ERA and a 0.70 WHIP across 72.7 AA innings isn't a hot stretch — it's a sustained demolition, and the strikeout-to-walk shape underneath it is what makes the number believable. Anderson has walked 10 batters all year against 108 strikeouts, and the translation puts his BB/9 at 2.1 in MLB context while the league sits at 3.2, so the command isn't a minor-league mirage. The whole percentile stack, ERA, WHIP, BB/9, K-BB%, grades at 99 against his pitcher pool, which means the dominance is broad rather than driven by one inflated rate. Mid-rotation starter is the projection floor; the question is whether the stuff that plays this cleanly at Double-A holds its shape against major-league hitters, and if it does, the ceiling is something considerably better.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is that the contact metrics and the power metrics are pulling in opposite directions. His 52.6% hard-hit rate sits at the 95th percentile, and his xBA of .280 suggests he earns his hits, but a 28.9% whiff rate undercuts the raw contact quality and explains why the xSLG lands at .420 rather than somewhere scarier. The projection settles him at .276/.346/.410 over 697 plate appearances, which is a useful everyday player — not a superstar line, but one propped up by 36 projected steals and fielding that grades out in the 91st percentile wherever he's stationed. The whole profile hinges on whether the whiff rate creeps down enough to let that exit velocity translate more consistently, because right now he's a plus athlete with plus contact quality who leaks too many swings against air.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile on Henderson is a puzzle: 44.7% hard-hit rate sitting comfortably above average, yet an xwOBA of .308 that ranks well below it. The disconnect lives in contact quality that doesn't translate — his 7.3% barrel rate and .391 xSLG suggest the loud contact isn't quite loud enough, often, and a 32.4% chase rate is bleeding the walk rate down to 7.7%, which kills the on-base side of the ledger. The projection (.238/.312/.425, 28 HR across a full 714 PA) reads like a shortstop who produces in counting stats because the position and the lineup do some of the work, not because the underlying hit tool is carrying its weight. Everything here hinges on whether the chase rate comes down; if it does, the hard-hit profile has real upside to grow into, but if it stays where it is, you're looking at a second-division regular with pop and speed who doesn't quite get on base enough to make it sing.

The walk rate is the engine here: 15% across 489 AA plate appearances, translating to 12.3% in MLB-equivalent context while the league sits at 8.5%. That's a real approach at a level where most hitters don't find the zone that honestly. The ISO sits at .168 in AA, but the translation softens it to .135, and the MLB average is .150, so the power is more fringe-average than the raw line suggests.

The profile hinges on whether that strikeout rate, 25.5% in translation versus a 22.0% MLB average, compresses as he climbs, because a DH without plus power needs to make contact often enough to keep the OBP from being his whole offensive argument. If it holds, he's a patient, line-drive-oriented bench or platoon bat who can work counts; if the strikeouts tick up against better stuff, the org-depth floor is right there.
reports.report: The walks create an everyday path, but the present outcome is a reserve; he forces pitchers into the zone and takes the free pass. The line does not show a second offensive strength at the same level. The latest meaningful sample is from 2025, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Elmer Rodríguez

reports.published_report: The 2.90 ERA across 66.3 AAA innings is the loudest number in this profile, but it's carrying weight the peripherals won't fully support. His MLB-equivalent walk rate translates to 4.2 per nine against a 3.2 MLB average — the walks are a real problem, and the strikeouts don't compensate, with his K/9 translating to 8.3 while the MLB average sits at 8.6. Run prevention graded 60 on the skill shape, miss and command both graded 40, which tells you what's happening: he's limiting damage without truly missing bats or commanding the zone, and that combination gets exposed quickly against better lineups. If the ERA holds up into a big-league role, it's as a multi-inning or setup arm; if the walk rate doesn't tighten, what's left is a depth piece.

reports.name: Cade Cavalli
reports.published_report: The fastball lives at 96.7 mph, which is loud, but the Statcast contact profile tells a quieter story: a 4.16 xERA sitting right at the league median, and a hard-hit rate of 40.1% that undercuts what the strikeout numbers promise. Cavalli punches out batters at a 25.4% clip and limits free passes at 7.4%, a genuine two-skill combination that keeps him viable in a rotation, yet the underlying contact quality hasn't rewarded that stuff the way you'd want. The projection lands him at a 3.82 ERA over 158.8 innings, which is a rotation contributor, but it's optimistic relative to what Statcast says hitters are actually doing to him. Everything hinges on whether the heater starts generating weaker contact, because the strikeout-to-walk foundation is real enough to carry a mid-rotation arm if the barrel suppression follows.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling two different stories, and the gap is the whole read. His xERA sits at 4.55 with a 9.7 BB% that rates in the bottom third of the league, yet the ValuCast projection has him at 3.65 ERA over 180.8 innings, which is a meaningful vote of confidence in his ability to keep outrunning his peripherals. What makes that bet plausible is the contact suppression: average exit velocity of 87.3 mph and a Hard-Hit% of 33.4% that actually rank well above league average, meaning when hitters do make contact, they're not squaring him up cleanly. The profile hinges entirely on whether the walk rate comes back down, because a 9.7 BB% paired with a strikeout rate of 20.8% leaves almost no margin for error in the rotation.

reports.name: Carson Benge
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at the 91st percentile is the loudest thing in this profile, and it matters because the contact quality isn't coming from elite exit velocity — his 89.4 mph average and 41.2% hard-hit rate are both near the middle of the league. He's putting the ball where fielders aren't, which is a skill, but it's a skill that lives and dies with batted-ball luck over a full season. The projection (.259/.323/.400 over 599 PA) reads like a league-average outfielder with a little pop and genuine wheels, 22 projected steals backing up what 28.5 ft/s sprint speed already tells you. His 7.4% walk rate is the quiet drag on the profile; if pitchers ever make him earn his way on base rather than roping singles, the .323 OBP gets fragile fast.

He's a second-division regular whose value lives and dies with the barrel rate holding.

reports.name: Kyle Bradish
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what keeps this from being a clean profile. Bradish's Statcast card reads like a league-average starter across the board, with a 3.79 xERA and a 23.3% strikeout rate that doesn't quite compensate for an 11.0% walk rate sitting in the 21st percentile. The contact he allows isn't catastrophic, an 8.2% barrel rate and 88.0 mph average exit velocity suggest he manages barrels well enough, but that BB% puts a ceiling on how deep he can go in games and explains why the projection lands at 176.0 innings with a 1.34 WHIP rather than something cleaner. If the walks tighten, a 3.72 ERA over that workload puts him squarely in mid-rotation territory; if they don't, he's a back-end starter eating innings but bleeding counts.

reports.name: TJ Rumfield
reports.published_report: The contact and plate discipline profile is legitimately useful, 13.8% strikeouts and 10.4% walks both well above the league baseline at their respective ends, but the power underneath it is genuinely thin, and that's the tension here. An 83.8 mph average exit velocity puts him at the 1st percentile; the 28.2% hard-hit rate is nearly as stark. He makes contact, avoids strikeouts at a rate most first basemen can't match, and draws enough walks to push an OBP projection of .366, but the .379 xSLG says the ball isn't leaving the yard consistently, and 18 projected home runs at Coors is a floor, not a ceiling. The whole profile rests on whether a first baseman who doesn't punish mistakes can hold value at the position; if the exit velocity doesn't move, he's a high-OBP second-division regular whose defense grades out well enough (84th percentile OAA) to keep him on a roster without ever threatening to carry one.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: A 23.0% chase rate is the engine here, genuinely elite plate discipline that keeps Suzuki in counts long enough to do damage despite a strikeout rate that climbs to 25.7%. The contact itself is middling, 89.0 mph average exit velocity and 40.6% hard-hit, but a 9.2% barrel rate translates that modest raw power into projected 25 home runs and a .455 projected SLG, which is the honest upside of a hitter who hunts good pitches rather than overwhelming ones. The whole profile hinges on that chase rate holding; if pitchers find a way to exploit him inside the zone, the strikeout exposure has nowhere to hide and the .343 projected OBP crumbles with it. Fully healthy in a near-full projection of 594 PA, he profiles as a solid everyday corner piece, not a lineup centerpiece, but a quietly above-average regular whose value lives in the walk and the barrel, not the bat speed.

reports.name: Xander Bogaerts
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a study in contradictions. Bogaerts runs an 11.3% walk rate and chases just 25.0% of pitches outside the zone, two marks that put him comfortably above league average in plate discipline, yet his 88.1 mph average exit velocity and 6.4% barrel rate both sit around the 30th percentile, which is why the underlying contact numbers look like a replacement-level hitter rather than a former All-Star. The discipline keeps him from being a drain on an at-bat, but without the bat speed to translate that patience into damage, a .315 xwOBA is the ceiling of what the approach buys him. The projection calls for a .682 OPS across 623 PA, which is a second-division regular at best, a soft regular who stays useful only as long as the walk rate and the 96th-percentile OAA at short prop up what the bat can no longer carry.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells two very different stories depending on which half you're reading. His 27.8% strikeout rate and 29.4% whiff rate say he misses bats at a genuine clip, the chase rate backs it up, and a 3.48 xERA suggests the underlying contact quality is well in his favor — but 91.7 mph fastball velocity and 2184 rpm spin sit near the bottom of the league, which means every bit of that swing-and-miss is earned through deception and location rather than stuff. The 8.9% walk rate is the friction point: the profile only works if he can keep threading the zone without a premium heater to bail him out when counts go wrong. If the command holds, he's a back-end starter who outperforms his raw stuff; if it slips, the 115 projected innings almost certainly migrate toward the bullpen, where the 10 projected holds already hint that Tampa is hedging.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The 34.5% chase rate is the engine here — that's well above the league norm, and it's why the .286 xwOBA and 3.36 xERA look legitimate despite a strikeout rate that sits right around league average at 22.9%. He gets hitters to chase, limits free passes at 6.8%, and the contact allowed is manageable at 87.9 mph average exit velocity. The whole profile hinges on that chase rate holding: if hitters start laying off, the modest swing-and-miss at 27.8% whiff rate isn't a fallback weapon, and the barrel rate at 9.0% suggests he can get hurt when they do connect. A mid-rotation innings-eater who profiles as a 3.54 ERA workhorse if the chase rate sustains, or a backend arm fighting for a rotation spot if it regresses.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the only part of this profile that isn't a problem. Across AA & A+, Gary Gill Hill's 2.1 BB/9 translates to a 2.7 MLB-equivalent figure, well below what most MLB starters allow, and that command grade of 75 is real enough to keep him in rotation discussions. The trouble is that he misses almost nobody: 71 strikeouts across 90.3 innings produces a 7.1 K/9 that translates to 6.7 at the MLB level, and the K-BB% shrinks from 13% in the minors to 10.5 against big-league hitters. Everything here hinges on whether the command advantage is durable enough to survive without swing-and-miss, because if that walk rate creeps upward even modestly there is no strikeout floor to catch it. The projection ceiling is a back-end starter or late-inning arm with a depth floor, which is an honest read on a 21-year-old who throws strikes but doesn't overpower anyone.
